paras: The 1903 Morgan Park lynching attempt and expulsion order was an attack by a white mob on Black prisoners in the village lockup of Morgan Park, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago, on November 1, 1903, followed by placards ordering all Black residents to leave. The prisoners, accused of killing police chief George A. Airey on Halloween, were rescued by Chicago police; after the placards several Black families left.

Airey, 65, had been Morgan Park's town marshal, or chief of police, for two years, according to the Polish-language Chicago daily Dziennik Chicagoski. On Halloween night, Saturday, October 31, a group of Black young people in costume were out on the village streets, among them Mack Wiley and his sister, Hattie Payne.

Accounts of the encounter differ. In the wire version, Airey, 'it is said,' struck Payne while her group overturned a lumber pile, and in a later fight Wiley stabbed him in the neck. Dziennik Chicagoski said Airey and a special officer, A. McPhee, tried to arrest the group believing they were stealing sidewalk boards, and one of them stabbed Airey three times; two briefs said he was shot.

On Sunday morning Wiley, 20, was arrested at Harvey, and Henry Lowry, James W. Payne, Alonzo Payne and Hattie Payne were also locked up at Morgan Park. A crowd that the wire put at 'half a hundred men and boys,' from Morgan Park, Harvey and Blue Island, gathered at the village hall. Led by John and Robert Airey, the chief's brother and son, it forced its way inside to the bars of the cell. A patrol wagon of Chicago police drove the mob back and took the four men to the Englewood station, but by then they had been 'severely cut and bruised with sticks and stones.'

On the evening of November 2, according to a New York Sun dispatch, men of the town met in secret and decided to clear Morgan Park of its Black population. Despite efforts by Mayor George Prentiss and twelve deputies, posters went up that night giving Black residents 48 hours to leave. Several families left, taking whatever goods they could carry.

At Englewood the men were said to have confessed and were held for the coroner's jury, whose verdict does not appear in the coverage. No arrests of mob members or of those who posted the placards were reported. On November 7 the Chicago Broad Ax wrote that whites had decided not to drive all Black residents from their homes.

In May 1904 Wiley was sentenced to life and Hattie Payne to an indeterminate term at Joliet. Dziennik Chicagoski reported that the jury had voted for hanging and Judge Smith changed it to life, and that Payne cried out in court that she, not her brother, had killed Airey.

White papers carried two wire stories. The first, headed 'Chicago Negroes Are Nearly Lynched for a Murder' in St. Paul and 'RACE RIOT' in Fargo, spoke of 'a threatened race war' and 'an armed mob of enraged whites.' The Watertown Republican's 'LYNCHING PREVENTED' credited Chicago police with saving Cook County 'from the disgrace that attends a lynching' while calling Airey's opponents 'a gang of disorderly negroes.'

The second, from November 3, ran as 'ALL NEGROES ORDERED TO LEAVE A TOWN' in Butte and 'NEGROES WARNED TO GO' in New York, presenting the order as 'the outcome of the murder' without naming who posted it. It reached Georgia as 'NEGRGES [Negroes] LEAVING CHICAGO' and shrank to one line in news summaries.

In the Black press, the Savannah Tribune gave the killing and the lynch mob one sentence in its 'Cream of News' column, without the placards. The Chicago Broad Ax called the killing 'a very unfortunate affair' and said the Black men responsible should be punished 'to the full extent of the law.' It found it 'refreshing' that whites would not class all Black people alike and drive them out, but said nothing of the attack on the prisoners. In 1904 it turned Hattie Payne's case into a warning to women 'both black and white' not to wear men's clothing on Halloween.

The mob attack is reported independently by the Polish-language Chicago daily, two wire versions and the Black press (A1, A2, A4, A12), and the placards by two separate dispatches and the Broad Ax (A5, A8, A13).

accounts.gist: Airey, 'it is said', struck Mrs. James Payne while she and friends overturned a lumber pile; at a second meeting Wiley stabbed him in the neck; an armed mob of whites nearly lynched the prisoners, who were cut and bruised before police removed them.

accounts.label: Dziennik Chicagoski (local)
accounts.gist: Airey and special officer McPhee tried to arrest a costumed group they thought was stealing sidewalk boards; one man stabbed Airey three times; police held off the crowd with revolvers until a Chicago patrol wagon took the men to Englewood.

accounts.label: Variant dispatch
accounts.gist: Airey was shot by a Black man he had arrested for Halloween pranks.

accounts.label: Black press summary
accounts.gist: A girl's prank led the chief to strike her; her brother killed him; officers got him to jail ahead of a lynch mob.

accounts.label: Hattie Payne in court
accounts.gist: At sentencing she cried that she, not her brother, had killed Airey; the paper reported Airey had struck her believing she was a man.

framing.detail: 'KILL POLICE CHIEF / Chicago Negroes Are Nearly Lynched for a Murder' and 'a threatened race war'; the Fargo paper headed it 'RACE RIOT.'
'LYNCHING PREVENTED' credits Chicago police with saving Cook County 'from the disgrace that attends a lynching' while calling the accused 'a gang of disorderly negroes'.
Placard stories ('ALL NEGROES ORDERED TO LEAVE A TOWN', 'NEGROES WARNED TO GO') present the order as 'the outcome of the murder' and the Black residents as 'stricken with terror'.
The Savannah Tribune carried a one-sentence wire summary among other news items, without the placards.

The Chicago Broad Ax called the killing 'a very unfortunate affair', urged full punishment of the Black men responsible, and called it 'refreshing' that whites would not drive all Black people from Morgan Park.
In 1904 the Broad Ax reported the sentences and turned Hattie Payne's case into a warning to women not to wear men's clothing on Halloween.
